entities.name: Makkhali Gosala
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Makkhali Gosala, also known as Manthaliputra Goshalak, emerged in the 6th century BCE as a prominent ascetic teacher and the leader of the Ajivika school of thought in ancient India. Flourishing during a period of intense intellectual and spiritual ferment in the Magadha region, Gosala was a direct contemporary of two of India's most influential religious founders: Gautama Buddha, who established Buddhism, and Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara of Jainism. His philosophical tenets, characterized by a radical fatalism (niyati), posited that all events, including individual destinies, are entirely predetermined and beyond human agency, offering a stark contrast to the doctrines of karma and free will central to competing traditions.

Gosala's early life is shrouded in legend, with traditional accounts from Buddhist and Jain texts often portraying him in an adversarial light. He is said to have been born in a cow shed (makhkhala) to a mendicant, hence his name. After a period of initial asceticism, he became a disciple of Purana Kassapa, another heterodox teacher, before establishing his own distinct Ajivika community. The Ajivikas, known for their extreme ascetic practices and nude renunciant lifestyle, gained considerable following, particularly among the merchant classes of the Gangetic plains, demonstrating a significant alternative to the Brahmanical orthodoxy and the emerging Sramanic traditions. Gosala himself is recorded to have died around 484 BCE in Shravasti, following a ritual called 'six-fold abstinence,' after a period of intense rivalry with Mahavira.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Makkhali Gosala, as the leader of the Ajivika school, significantly contributed to the diverse philosophical landscape of ancient India, offering a radical fatalistic doctrine that challenged the prevailing concepts of karma and free will. His teachings attracted a substantial following for over 1000 years, influencing the intellectual and religious discourse of the subcontinent.
